publication_scope.blurb: Louis Le Blanc de Beaulieu - Sedan Theological Theses, newly rendered from the 1675 London Latin. Covers De Theologia through Angelorum & Hominum Sanctorum Cultu Romana I-LXXVII and Pars Secunda (Reformata) I-CI, De Primi Hominis Immortalitate I-XXXV, De Justitia Primi Hominis I-LIX, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio in genere I-XLVIII, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio absolute & in se spectato (Scholae Romanae doctrina I-XLIX; Pars Tertia I-XLIII), the theses on reconciling divine concurrence with human freedom I-LIX, on human freedom and divine foreknowledge I-XLIV, and on human freedom and the divine decrees, Part One (middle knowledge) I-LXV, Part Two (the Roman doctors) I-XXXVI and Part Three (the Reformed) I-LI, and on how fallen man's free choice stands toward saving good (I-LX), and on the necessity of grace for moral good in fallen man (Pars Prior I-LIII; Pars Posterior, the Protestant doctrine, I-LIX), and on the various distinctions and senses of grace in the Roman School (I-LXX) and in the Reformed Schools (I-XLIX), and on the Roman School's division of grace into sufficient and efficacious (I-CXLV, complete), and on the Protestant doctrine of that distinction, the Lutherans of the Augsburg Confession, the Remonstrants, and the Reformed who subscribe to Dort, with the Reformed debate on how grace moves the will (I-LXVI). Not the collected folio.
publication_scope.era_note: Le Blanc wrote in the mid-seventeenth century as Reformed professor at the Academy of Sedan. This is not a patristic work. It is a public-domain Latin Reformed retrieval on the same Fathers-site pipeline. The 1675 Pitt folio is Public Domain Mark 1.0. Do not treat the site as ante-Nicene only.

source_text: L. Porro quamvis Scholae Reformatae Doctores in eo conveniant gratiam non tantum in hominis mentem, sed etiam in voluntatem efficaciam suam exerere, eamque potenter & infallibiliter ad bonum flectere & determinare: inter eos tamen est aliquis dissensus de modo quo gratia voluntatem nostram movet, ut in Deum feratur, & bono consentiat.
english: Thesis L. Further, the teachers of the Reformed school all agree that grace exerts its efficacy not just on the human mind but on the will as well, and that it bends and settles the will toward the good with power and without fail.
Where they part company is over how grace moves our will so that it turns toward God and gives its assent to what is good.

source_text: LI. Nam Paulus Testardus, & Moses Amyraldus, aliique qui cum iis in gratiae negotio Cameronis Methodum & doctrinam sequuntur, efficaciam gratiae divinae, quae hominem ad Deum convertit, eique fidem in Christum ingenerat, & Dei amore cor illius accendit, in eo consistere docent, quod salutaris veritas in Evangelio proposita eo modo menti offeratur, & arcana virtute spiritus mens intus ita disponatur, ut homo firmissimam & efficacissimam veritatis illius persuasionem inde concipiat, statuatque nihil melius, & ad veram beatitudinem obtinendam conducibilius, quam ut quis Christo adhaereat, & Evangelio illius obsequatur. Unde fit ut voluntas, quae ex eorum hypothesi, necessario sequitur ductum & judicium intellectus practici, bonum illud salutare per Evangelium oblatum, & ab intellectu monstratum suscipiat, atque avide complectatur: & sic a rebus vanis & terrenis aversa tota convertatur ad Deum, qua in re consistit ejus innovatio & sanctificatio.
english: Thesis LI. Paulus Testardus, Moses Amyraldus and the others who follow Camero's method and teaching on grace hold that the efficacy of God's grace, which turns a person to God, plants faith in Christ in him and sets his heart on fire with love for God, works like this. The saving truth set out in the Gospel is presented to the mind in a certain way, and the Spirit's hidden power so shapes the mind from within that the person comes to be utterly and effectively convinced of that truth.

He concludes that nothing is better, and nothing does more to bring a person to true happiness, than holding fast to Christ and obeying his Gospel. On their premise the will must follow where the practical intellect leads and what it judges, so the will takes up the saving good that the Gospel offers and the intellect points out, and grasps it eagerly. Turned away from empty and earthly things, it turns wholly to God, and in this its renewal and sanctification consist.

source_text: LII. Adeoque volunt illi efficaciam gratiae divinae primario & immediate in solam mentem sese exerere, in affectus autem atque voluntatem consequenter solum & secundario: sic ut renovatio voluntatis & affectuum non fiat, nisi mediante intellectus renovatione, dum ad eas facultates, intellectus ductui subjectas, lucis mentem renovantis fructus & ἐνέργεια pervenit. Ut videre est apud Paulum Testardum in Irenico thesi 424. & sequentibus.
english: Thesis LII. So they hold that the efficacy of God's grace exerts itself first and directly on the mind alone, and on the affections and the will only as a result and at second hand. The will and affections are renewed only through the renewing of the intellect, as the fruit and working (energeia) of the light that renews the mind passes on to those faculties, which are subject to the intellect's lead.
This can be seen in Paulus Testardus, Irenicum, thesis 424 and following.

source_text: LIII. Ex dictis vero patet eorum sententiam non parum discrepare ab opinione illorum qui sentiunt totam gratiae efficaciam sitam esse in morali quadam suasione, quae voluntatem relinquat in indifferentia, & possit ab illa rejici, vel admitti. In iis enim qui per Dei gratiam convertuntur, non solum agnoscunt quandam spiritus Dei per verbum operantis suasionem, sed vehementem plane & fortem persuasionem, quae voluntatem secum rapit & efficacissime movet, ac suavissime quidem, sed certo tamen & infallibiliter ad bonum determinat, & consensum ab ea exprimit, non vero tanquam a dubia & indifferenti expectat.
english: Thesis LIII. It is clear from this that their view is quite different from that of people who place the whole efficacy of grace in a kind of moral persuasion, one that leaves the will undecided and can be either accepted or rejected by it.

In those who are converted by God's grace they recognize not only some persuading by God's Spirit working through the word, but a truly forceful and strong persuasion that sweeps the will along and moves it with the greatest effect: very gently indeed, yet surely and without fail it settles the will on the good and draws its consent out of it, instead of waiting for consent as if from a will still doubtful and undecided.

source_text: LIV. Verum alii Scholae Reformatae Theologi volunt immediatam gratiae operationem non solum mentem attingere, dum eam illuminat, & nova luce perfundit, sed ipsam quoque voluntatem, in qua consensum illum, quem divinis monitis adhibet, realiter & Physice operatur.
english: Thesis LIV. Other theologians of the Reformed school, however, hold that grace acts directly not only on the mind, enlightening it and flooding it with new light, but on the will itself as well.
In the will, they say, grace really and physically produces the consent that the will gives to God's admonitions.

source_text: LV. Hanc sententiam tradit & explicat Amesius in Bellarmino enervato libro tertio de Gratia capite tertio. Nos dicimus, inquit, una cum suasione morali conjungi etiam realem efficientiam Dei, qua novum principium spiritualis vitae cordi hominis efficaciter vocati ingeneratur, & homo simul excitatur ad hujus vitae actus eliciendos.
english: Thesis LV. Amesius sets out and explains this view in Bellarminus enervatus, book 3, on grace, chapter 3. 'We say,' he writes, 'that along with moral persuasion there is also a real causal working of God.
By it a new source of spiritual life is planted in the heart of the person who is effectively called, and at the same time he is roused to perform the acts of this life.'

source_text: LVI. Ibidemque omnino probat, & ut suam agnoscit sententiam Didaci Alvarés, quae est, Deum per auxilium gratiae efficax Physice, sive ad modum causae Physicae praedeterminare arbitrium creatum, ut infallibiliter consentiat & cooperetur Deo vocanti atque excitanti. Posteaque ipsius Alvarés verbis utens, dicit Physice praedeterminare nihil aliud esse, quam vere, efficienter, vel realiter facere, ut ipsum arbitrium infallibiliter Deo cooperetur. Et Auxilium gratiae ex se efficax, prout venit a Deo antecedenter ad liberam cooperationem arbitrii, & auxilium Physice praedeterminans idem significare.
english: Thesis LVI. In the same place he fully approves Didacus Alvarez's view and owns it as his own: through the efficacious help of grace God physically predetermines the created will, that is, in the manner of a physical cause, so that it consents without fail and works together with God as he calls and rouses it.

Then, in Alvarez's own words, he says that to predetermine physically is nothing other than truly, efficiently or really to make the will itself work together with God without fail. He adds that 'help of grace efficacious of itself', as it comes from God ahead of the will's free cooperation, and 'help that predetermines physically' mean the same thing.

source_text: LVII. Quantumcunque vero tum hi tum illi Scholae Reformatae Doctores efficaciam gratiae divinae exaggerent, nolunt tamen illam quicquam humanae voluntatis libertati praejudicare, sed quaecunque bona opera per Dei gratiam ab homine fiunt, ab iis libere fieri, adeoque primum ipsum actum conversionis non minus liberum esse, quam qui eum sequuntur, nec solum esse vitalem voluntatis nostrae operationem, sed ab ea libere elici.
english: Thesis LVII. Yet however much both groups of Reformed teachers stress the efficacy of God's grace, they deny that it in any way harms the freedom of the human will. Whatever good works a person does by God's grace, he does freely.
So the very first act of conversion is just as free as the acts that follow it: it is not merely a living operation of our will but one the will freely brings forth.

source_text: LVIII. Quomodo vero ista inter se constent, non eadem ratione omnes ostendere conantur. Et quidem modo citatus Amesius sic post Didacum Alvarés conciliare nititur immediatam illam & efficacem gratiae divinae in voluntatem operationem & determinationem, cum voluntatis ipsius libertate in agendo, & gratiae obsequendo. Nempe libere operari dicit illum qui dum agit retinet potestatem non agendi. Jam vero gratiam, quamvis voluntatem moveat & determinet ad agendum, ab ea tamen non tollere non agendi potestatem. Quippe potentiam ad non operandum simul consistere in eodem subjecto cum gratia & auxilio quod requiritur ad operandum, & efficit ut aliquis operetur: licet simul nunquam sint nec esse possint in eodem subjecto gratia & auxilium ad talem operationem particularem datum, & carentia talis actus. Quod alii dicunt gratiam actum quidem determinare, sed tamen a facultate non tollere omnem indifferentiam & indeterminationem.
english: Thesis LVIII. Not all of them, however, show in the same way how these things fit together. Amesius, just cited, following Didacus Alvarez, tries to reconcile that direct and effective working and determining of God's grace in the will with the will's own freedom in acting and in obeying grace.

He says that someone acts freely if, while acting, he keeps the power not to act. Grace moves and determines the will to act, yet it does not take away its power not to act. The power not to act exists in the same subject together with the grace and help needed for acting, the help that makes someone act.

Yet the grace and help given for a particular action and the absence of that action never are, and never can be, in the same subject at once. Others say the same thing this way: grace does determine the act, but it does not remove all indifference and indetermination from the faculty.

source_text: LIX. Illi vero priores qui Cameronis doctrinam sequuntur, ex sua hypothesi, non difficulter ostendi posse putant quomodo certa & infallibilis, & a voluntatis nostrae consensu minime dependens gratiae operatio cum libertate humana optime consentiat. Nam juxta eorum doctrinam, certa & infallibilis est illa operatio, quoniam mens rite affecta, & sese habens naturae congruenter, non potest verum oblatum & agnitum non amplecti, & non judicare bonum id cujus bonitas ipsi in aperto ponitur: quandoquidem ex convenienti appulsu & applicatione objecti ad facultatem, quae recte se habet, necessario sequitur operatio naturae conveniens. Et similiter voluntas non potest non velle & sequi id quod, omnibus expensis, intellectus volendum & sequendum judicat.
english: Thesis LIX. The first group, Camero's followers, think their premise makes it easy to show how a working of grace that is sure and infallible, and in no way depends on our will's consent, fits perfectly with human freedom.

On their teaching that working is sure and infallible because a mind in the right state, acting in keeping with its nature, cannot fail to embrace the truth when it is offered and recognized, or fail to judge good what is plainly shown to be good. When an object is fittingly brought to bear on a faculty that is in good order, an action in keeping with its nature follows by necessity.
In the same way the will cannot fail to will and follow what the intellect, having weighed everything, judges is to be willed and followed.

source_text: LX. Neque tamen quicquam hic officit libertati, sive ex parte intellectus, sive ex parte voluntatis. Non ex parte intellectus, quia erga ipsum gratia haec duo tantum praestat, primo ut Evangelica veritas in convenienti luce ipsi proponatur: Deinde ut in statum congruentem restituatur, aut etiam aliquantum supra naturae sortem evehatur. Licet autem intellectus non possit vero agnito assensum non praebere, nulla tamen vis ipsi a proposita veritate affertur, dum assentitur vero, & in eo naturae suae maxime congruenter agit: ac proinde si qua species libertatis ipsi competit, hac in parte nihil laeditur. Et multo minus interna gratiae operatio, quae aut amissas vires intellectui restituit, aut etiam novas sufficit, praejudicare potest libertati intellectus, si quam habere censetur.
english: Thesis LX. Nothing here harms freedom, they say, either in the intellect or in the will. Not in the intellect, since grace does only two things for it: it sets the Gospel truth before it in a fitting light, and it restores it to a fitting condition, or even lifts it somewhat above its natural lot.

The intellect cannot withhold assent from a truth it has recognized, but the truth put before it does it no violence when it assents, since in assenting it acts entirely in keeping with its nature. So if the intellect has any sort of freedom, that freedom suffers no harm here.
Still less can the inward working of grace, which gives back to the intellect the powers it had lost or even supplies new ones, damage whatever freedom the intellect is thought to have.

source_text: LXI. Ex parte vero voluntatis, quanquam quae descripta est gratiae operatio, necessario ejus consensum eliciat, nullatenus tamen illi libertatem adimit. Nec enim voluntatem movet, & determinat, nisi per intellectus practici judicium. Sed ex virorum illorum doctorum sententia, necessitas & determinatio actuum voluntatis, quae ex mentis practicae judicio oritur, non obstat quominus libere a voluntate procedant: quandoquidem libertas voluntatis non opponitur cuivis necessitati, sed illi tantum, quae est a vi externa, a materia, vel a sensu. Quae latius diducta videre est apud Mosen Amyraldum tractatu de libero arbitrio, praecipue Sectione quarta. Et similiter in libro posthumo Josuae Placei de eodem argumento.
english: Thesis LXI. As for the will, the working of grace described above does necessarily draw out its consent, yet it in no way takes its freedom away, since it moves and determines the will only through the judgment of the practical intellect.

In these learned men's view, the necessity and determination of the will's acts that come from the mind's practical judgment do not stop those acts from proceeding freely from the will. The will's freedom is not opposed to every necessity, only to necessity that comes from outside force, from matter or from the senses.
This is argued more fully in Moses Amyraldus' treatise on free will, especially section 4, and likewise in Josua Placeus' posthumous book on the same subject.

source_text: LXII. Sed vetustiores Scholae Reformatae Doctores simplicius respondent gratiam non tollere a voluntate libertatem, licet aliquam ei necessitatem imponat, quia non omnis necessitas cum libertate pugnat, sed ea solum quae est a vi externa, vel a naturali determinatione. Gratia vero voluntatem non cogit, neque vim ei ullam affert, sed illam suaviter flectit, & modo qui est ejus naturae consentaneus.
english: Thesis LXII. The older teachers of the Reformed school give a simpler answer. Grace does not take freedom away from the will, even though it lays a certain necessity on it, because not every necessity is at odds with freedom, only the necessity that comes from outside force or from natural determination.
Grace does not compel the will or do it any violence; it bends it gently, in a way that suits its nature.

source_text: LXIII. Porro quod fatentur Scholae Reformatae Doctores, hominem qui per Dei gratiam convertitur, libere ipsum primum conversionis actum elicere, prima specie satis concordare non videtur, cum eo quod communiter docent, idque cum Theologis confessionis Augustanae, videlicet, hominem ad opus regenerationis & conversionis suae mere passive se habere. Quomodo enim voluntas humana potest conversionis actum libere elicere, & simul tamen ad sui conversionem mere passive se habere? an mere passive se habet voluntas quae supponitur libere operari?
english: Thesis LXIII. The Reformed teachers also admit that a person converted by God's grace freely performs the very first act of conversion. At first sight this does not seem to fit well with what they commonly teach, in agreement with the theologians of the Augsburg Confession: that in the work of his regeneration and conversion a person is merely passive.
How can the human will freely perform the act of conversion and yet be merely passive in its own conversion? Can a will that is assumed to act freely be merely passive?

source_text: LXIV. Hunc nodum solvunt Theologi Britanni in explicatione suae sententiae circa tertium & quartum articulum, actis Synodi Dordrechtanae inserta. Ubi observant conversionem duplici sensu sumi. Et primo quidem denotare immediatum opus Dei hominem regenerantis. Secundo denotare actionem hominis per fidem & poenitentiam salutiferam se ad Deum convertentis. Ad opus conversionis, sive regenerationis primo modo sumptae homo, juxta ipsos, se habet passive, neque est in potestate voluntatis humanae impedire Deum sic immediate convertentem & regenerantem. In conversione vero secundo modo accepta voluntas acta a Deo agit, actusque, quibus constat nostra ad Deum conversio, elicit.
english: Thesis LXIV. The British theologians untie this knot in the explanation of their opinion on the third and fourth articles that is included in the Acts of the Synod of Dort. They point out that 'conversion' is used in two senses.

First, it means the direct work of God by which he regenerates a person; second, the act by which a person turns himself to God through faith and saving repentance. In conversion or regeneration in the first sense, on their account, a person is passive, and it is not in the human will's power to hinder God as he thus directly converts and regenerates.
In conversion in the second sense the will, moved by God, does act, and it performs the acts that make up our turning to God.

source_text: LXV. Caeterum conversionem prout immediatum opus Dei designat, dicunt esse qua Deus animos electorum suorum prius variis actibus gratiae suae excitatos & praeparatos, intima quadam, & mirabili operatione regenerat, & quasi de novo creat; infundendo spiritum vivificantem & omnes animae facultates novis qualitatibus imbuendo. Hanc vero conversionem, ex eorum sensu, sequitur, non tempore sed natura, nostra conversio actualis, Deo proliciente ipsum actum credendi & convertendi ex mutata voluntate, quo acta a Deo agit & ipsa, convertendo se ad Deum & credendo, hoc est, actum suum vitalem eliciendo. Addunt divinam illam actionem non laedere voluntatis libertatem, sed roborare: nec extirpare radicitus vitiosam resistendi possibilitatem; sed efficaciter & suaviter dare homini firmam obediendi voluntatem.
english: Thesis LXV. Conversion in the sense of God's direct work, they say, is the work by which God, through an innermost and wonderful working, regenerates the souls of his elect, which various acts of his grace have already stirred and prepared, and as it were creates them anew, pouring in the life-giving Spirit and filling every faculty of the soul with new qualities.

In their view this conversion is followed, not in time but in order of nature, by our actual conversion: God draws the act of believing and turning out of the changed will, and the will, moved by God, then acts too, turning itself to God and believing, that is, producing its own living act.

They add that this divine action does not damage the will's freedom but strengthens it. It does not tear out by the roots the corrupt possibility of resisting, but effectively and gently gives the person a firm will to obey.

source_text: LXVI. Eodem redit quod docent Theologi Hassiaci in expositione suae sententiae circa articulum tertium & quartum, quae inserta quoque est actis ejusdem synodi. Ibi enim sic se habet eorum sexta thesis de homine in statu gratiae. Voluntas itaque hominis ad qualitates, seu facultates & vires supernaturales, nec non ad inclinationes novas recipiendas, habet se mere passive; ita ut actio Spiritus Sancti supernaturales illas vires in voluntatem infundentis, eandemque efficaciter & potenter ad conversionem & fidem flectentis & inclinantis, non a voluntate humana, ejusque cooperatione, vel consensu pendeat: Ad ipsos vero fidei, charitatis, spei, &c. actus, motusque bonos, non pure passive, sed passive & active se habet: cum Dei gratia praeveniente acta & mota, ac subsequente adjuta, ipsa etiam agat, fideique, charitatis, spei, aliarumque virtutum actus producat. Atque hinc non Deus in nobis, seu per nos, sed nos gratia Dei credere, sperare, diligere dicimur.
english: Thesis LXVI. The Hessian theologians teach the same thing in the exposition of their opinion on the third and fourth articles, which is also included in the Acts of that Synod. Their sixth thesis, on man in the state of grace, reads:

'The human will is therefore merely passive in receiving supernatural qualities, or faculties and powers, and new inclinations. The action of the Holy Spirit, who pours those supernatural powers into the will and bends and inclines it effectively and powerfully to conversion and faith, does not depend on the human will or on its cooperation or consent.

But with respect to the acts of faith, love, hope and so on, and to good motions, the will is not purely passive but both passive and active. Moved and stirred by God's preceding grace and helped by his following grace, it acts too, and produces acts of faith, love, hope and the other virtues. That is why it is not said that God believes, hopes and loves in us or through us, but that we do so by God's grace.'
